newsitem.title: USA: Civil rights groups sue to block California measure.
newsitem.headline: Civil rights groups sue to block California measure.

text.p: Civil rights groups filed suit on Wednesday to block a California initiative scrapping many state affirmative action programmes a day after a majority of Californians voted for the measure.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other civil rights, business and education groups alleged in the suit filed in U.S. District Court in San Francisco that the measure, Proposition 209, violated the U.S. Constitution.

"No statewide measure in American history has ever come close in scope or effect to Proposition 209's chokehold on state and local government," said Mark Rosenbaum, legal director of the ACLU of Southern California.
Californians voted 54-46 percent on Tuesday for the measure, which strikes a blow at 30 years of U.S. affirmative action policies aimed at broadening opportunities for women and racial minorities.

The measure, also known as the California Civil Rights Initiative, bans state and local government affirmative action programmes in public employment, education and contracting in California that are based on race or sex.

Proposition 209 had an immediate impact. Judson King, provost of the University of California, sent a letter to the chancellors of the university's nine campuses, telling them that decisions on student admissions made from now on should not include consideration of race or sex.

The university had already decided to abolish racial preferences in undergraduate admissions for students entering in the spring of 1998. Now, the new policy will apply to students applying to enroll in the fall of 1997.

The civil rights groups argued in their lawsuit that Proposition 209 violates the equal protection clause of the constitution because it would block legislation needed to protect minorities and women from discrimination.
They alleged it also violates the supremacy clause of the Constitution by outlawing state and local programmes established to ensure compliance with federal civil rights laws.
No date has yet been set for a court hearing, an ACLU spokeswoman said.
Supporters of the initiative also filed suit on Wednesday, seeking an order to force three state agencies to implement Proposition 209 and scrap their affirmative action programmes.

The suit, filed in Sacramento County Superior Court, targets the hiring and contracting practices of the California Community Colleges, the State Lottery Commission and the Department of General Services.

At the University of California at Santa Cruz, a crowd of students ranging between 75 and 200 blocked entrances to an administration building on Wednesday in a peaceful demonstration against Proposition 209, a university spokesman said, while opponents in San Francisco planned a candlelight vigil on Wednesday evening.

The flurry of lawsuits and protests was reminiscent of the uproar that greeted the passage two years ago of another controversial California initiative to cut off services to illegal immigrants. That measure has been tied up in the courts ever since.

Tuesday's vote followed an emotional campaign, with Proposition 209 supporters saying racial and gender preferences discriminated against others who may be better qualified. Opponents said minorities and women still faced discrimination in education and the workplace and affirmative action policies were needed to "level the playing field."

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and California's Republican Gov. Pete Wilson supported the measure while President Bill Clinton, retired Gen. Colin Powell and civil rights leader Jesse Jackson were among those opposed.
